newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Credit Foncier swings into surprise profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Credit Foncier swings into surprise profit.

text.p: Distressed property lender Credit Foncier de France, due to be wound down by the state after posting huge losses last year, reported on Friday a surprise first-half return to profit.

Credit Foncier, one of the biggest victims of France's 1990 property crash, announced a 402 million French franc ($79.40 million) first-half profit compared with a 12 million franc loss and forecast a "positive" full year result barring a fresh real estate downturn.

The news drew a stinging response from a shareholders' action group which has demanded more than the 70 francs per share offered under the state-orchestrated takeover for the stock that once traded around 450 francs.

"This shows the need for an independent evaluation of Credit Foncier's worth," said Colette Neuville, head of the minority shareholders group ADAM. She said unless ADAM got an independent opinion, it would try legal means to block the takeover.

ADAM has charged that last year's 13.6 billion franc worth of property provisions which drove the 144-year-old lending institution to a 10.8 billion franc 1995 full-year loss were excessive and unnecessary and virtually wiped out their equity.

The government said in July that Credit Foncier, France's second-biggest bond issuer after the state, would be taken over by state bank CDC after CFF failed to find anyone in the private sector to salvage it.

Plans call for a "managed wind-down" of the bank under which its commmercial activities and low-cost housing loan portfolio would be spun off. CFF would be reduced to a shell company and placed in a state holding firm that would ensure some 260 francs worth of bonds issued in its name were honoured.

Until recently the bank, whose shares were suspended August 28, had been widely expected to post a 1996 loss of 520 million francs. It attributed its change in fortunes to falling interest rates and a better than expected real estate risk climate.
Credit Foncier said its board approved the rescue plan as the sole alternative option to a liquidation which it said would be disadvantageous for shareholders.

The first half results included provisions of 671 million francs, down from 1.3 billion francs in the year earlier period. Net banking income fell four percent to 2.2 billion francs while operating profit was stable at 975 million.
First-half profits were swelled by an exceptional gain of 96.9 million francs on the sale of municipal debt and capital gains of 37.3 million francs on sale of investment holdings.

The group, which was also hammered by the loss of a state monopoly to sell low-cost mortgages, is private but its top management is controlled by the government due to its status as a "specialised financial institution".
The takeover, which will cost around 2.5 billion francs, requires acceptances covering two-thirds of the shares.
